title: Renal Circulation
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows blood through the kidney and explains why its layout matters. Two capillary beds sit in series between two arterioles, so the tone of each arteriole sets renal plasma flow, glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and filtration fraction, and two intrinsic mechanisms hold GFR steady as blood pressure changes. The same anatomy explains disease: end arteries produce wedge-shaped infarcts, the slow and hypoxic vasa recta favor sickling and papillary necrosis, and the course of the left renal vein links a renal tumor to a left varicocele. Board questions ask you to predict a number or a lesion from the vessel involved, so focus on the reasoning from structure to consequence.

Nephron segments and the difference between cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons (UR-2)

connections.how: Glomerular and peritubular Starling forces depend directly on the arteriolar resistances described here.
The macula densa and juxtaglomerular cells that drive tubuloglomerular feedback also control renin release and the renin-angiotensin system.
Renal blood flow obeys flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance, and autoregulation is a renal case of local flow control.
Renal medullary conditions are severe enough to make red cells sickle even in sickle cell trait.

Passive exchange of water, solutes, and gases between closely apposed vessels carrying blood in opposite directions.

sections.title: The path of blood through the kidney

blocks.text: The kidneys make up about 0.5% of body weight but receive about 20 to 25% of the cardiac output at rest, roughly 1.1 to 1.2 L/min, which gives a renal plasma flow of about 650 mL/min. This flow far exceeds the kidneys' metabolic needs. Its purpose is to deliver plasma for filtration and processing, and about 90% of it goes to the cortex, where the glomeruli are; the medulla receives the remaining 10% or so.

Each renal artery leaves the aorta at about the level of the L1 to L2 intervertebral disc. Near the hilum it divides into anterior and posterior divisions that give rise to about five segmental arteries. Within the sinus these branch into interlobar arteries, which run through the renal columns between the pyramids. At the corticomedullary junction the interlobar arteries bend over the bases of the pyramids as arcuate arteries, and these send cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries outward toward the capsule. Each cortical radiate artery gives off afferent arterioles, and each afferent arteriole feeds one glomerulus.

blocks.caption: Two capillary beds lie in series, separated by the efferent arteriole.

blocks.text: The defining feature is two capillary beds in series, each with a resistance vessel on either side. Because the glomerular capillaries lie between the afferent and efferent arterioles, their hydrostatic pressure stays high, about 60 mm Hg, along their whole length, which favors filtration. The efferent arteriole then drops the pressure again, so the peritubular capillaries receive blood at about 13 mm Hg. That blood also has a high oncotic pressure, because about one fifth of the plasma water but almost none of the protein was removed in the glomerulus. Low hydrostatic and high oncotic pressure favor uptake of the fluid that the tubules reabsorb.

The second bed depends on nephron type. Efferent arterioles of cortical nephrons, which have short loops of Henle, break into peritubular capillaries around the cortical tubules. Efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, whose glomeruli lie near the corticomedullary junction and whose long loops reach deep into the medulla, form the vasa recta (C05). Blood returns through cortical radiate, arcuate, and interlobar veins to the renal vein. Unlike the arteries, the intrarenal veins anastomose freely, which matters for infarction (C02).

sections.title: End arteries and wedge-shaped renal infarcts

blocks.text: An end artery is the only arterial supply to its territory, so when it is blocked no neighboring vessel can carry enough blood in to keep the tissue alive. The segmental arteries divide the kidney into vascular segments that share no useful collateral flow, and the plane between the anterior and posterior segments is relatively avascular. The pattern continues inside the kidney: interlobar arteries do not connect with each other, the arcuate arteries arch over the pyramids without forming complete arcades, and cortical radiate arteries supply their own columns of nephrons. Accessory renal arteries, which enter a pole directly, are end arteries as well, so losing one infarcts that pole.

The usual cause is an embolus from the left side of the heart: thrombus from the left atrium in atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus after a myocardial infarction, or a fragment of an infective endocarditis vegetation. The embolus lodges where the artery becomes narrower than the embolus. Everything that artery supplies lies downstream and fans outward toward the capsule, so the dead tissue forms a cone, seen on the cut surface as a wedge with its base at the capsular surface and its apex pointing toward the medulla and hilum.

blocks.title: From embolus to wedge-shaped infarct
steps: Left atrial or ventricular thrombus fragments
Embolus lodges in a segmental or interlobar artery
No collateral flow reaches the territory
Ischemic coagulative necrosis of a cone of tissue
Pale wedge: base at capsule, apex toward medulla
Healing leaves a depressed cortical scar
blocks.caption: The infarct takes the shape of the occluded artery's territory.

blocks.text: Renal infarcts are pale (anemic). The kidney is a solid organ with a single arterial supply, so little blood seeps into the dead tissue, unlike the hemorrhagic infarcts of the lung, which has a dual supply, or of loose tissues such as bowel. Coagulative necrosis preserves the outlines of tubules and glomeruli for several days while the nuclei disappear. Within a day or two a hyperemic, inflamed border develops at the margin, and the infarct heals as a depressed, V-shaped fibrous scar. A thin rim of subcapsular cortex is often spared because capsular vessels supply it.

Manifestations follow from the necrosis: sudden flank pain, hematuria, and a rise in serum lactate dehydrogenase released from dead cells, although small infarcts may be silent. Two look-alikes are worth separating. Cholesterol atheroemboli, often after aortic instrumentation, lodge in small arcuate and cortical radiate arteries and cause many tiny patchy infarcts rather than one large wedge. Renal vein thrombosis produces a swollen, congested kidney rather than a pale wedge, because arterial inflow continues while outflow is blocked.

blocks.predict: An embolus blocks one cortical radiate artery. Predict the size and shape of the lesion compared with a segmental artery occlusion.
blocks.explain: A small wedge confined to the cortex. The cortical radiate artery is also an end artery, so the tissue it supplies dies, but its territory is a narrow column of cortex rather than a whole segment.
blocks.check: The description of end arteries and the shape of the infarct.

sections.title: Afferent and efferent arterioles: RPF, GFR, and filtration fraction

blocks.text: Renal blood flow equals the pressure difference between renal artery and renal vein divided by total renal vascular resistance, and most of that resistance lies in the afferent and efferent arterioles. GFR equals the filtration coefficient (Kf) multiplied by the net filtration pressure, which is glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman's space pressure minus glomerular oncotic pressure. Because the glomerulus sits between the two arterioles, its hydrostatic pressure behaves like the midpoint of two resistors in series: raising the upstream resistance lowers it, and raising the downstream resistance raises it. Both resistances add to total resistance, so constricting either one lowers flow.

blocks.title: Effects of arteriolar tone
blocks.caption: Afferent changes move RPF and GFR in the same direction; only efferent changes move them apart and so change filtration fraction.

blocks.text: Afferent constriction lowers both glomerular pressure and plasma flow, so GFR and RPF fall roughly in proportion and filtration fraction changes little. Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure, so GFR rises while total flow falls, and filtration fraction rises. The effect is biphasic. With strong efferent constriction, flow becomes so slow that plasma proteins concentrate rapidly along the capillary, glomerular oncotic pressure rises until it cancels the hydrostatic gradient, and GFR falls despite the high capillary pressure.

Filtration fraction also shapes reabsorption. A higher filtration fraction leaves postglomerular blood with a higher oncotic pressure and, after efferent constriction, a lower peritubular hydrostatic pressure, so the peritubular capillaries take up reabsorbed fluid from the proximal tubule more avidly.

blocks.title: How GFR is defended when renal perfusion falls
steps: Renal perfusion pressure falls
Prostaglandins and nitric oxide dilate the afferent arteriole

Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole

Losing either arm lets GFR fall
blocks.caption: Blocking prostaglandin synthesis (NSAIDs) removes the afferent arm; blocking angiotensin II formation or action removes the efferent arm.

blocks.text: When perfusion is low, as in volume depletion, heart failure, or bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends on both arms. Cyclooxygenase inhibition removes prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation, and blocking angiotensin II removes efferent constriction; either can then lower glomerular pressure enough to cause acute kidney injury.

blocks.title: Worked example: calculating filtration fraction
blocks.text: At baseline, RPF is 650 mL/min and GFR is 125 mL/min, so FF is 125 divided by 650, about 0.19. Angiotensin II then constricts the efferent arteriole moderately: RPF falls to 550 mL/min and GFR rises to 130 mL/min. FF is now 130 divided by 550, about 0.24. Filtration fraction rose for two reasons at once, because the numerator rose and the denominator fell. Compare afferent constriction that lowers RPF to 550 mL/min and GFR to about 106 mL/min: FF stays about 0.19, because both fell by about the same fraction. The illustrative numbers show the rule: only efferent changes move filtration fraction.

sections.title: Autoregulation: the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

blocks.text: Renal blood flow and GFR stay nearly constant while mean arterial pressure varies between about 75 and 160 mm Hg (some texts extend the upper limit to about 180 mm Hg). Since flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance, constant flow at a higher pressure requires a matching rise in resistance. The kidney adds that resistance mainly at the afferent arteriole, upstream of the glomerulus, so glomerular pressure and GFR are held along with flow. Without this, a 25% rise in pressure would raise GFR by about 25% and deliver far more filtrate than the tubules could reabsorb. Autoregulation is not perfect, and small changes in GFR and sodium excretion with pressure still occur.

The myogenic response is a property of the arteriolar wall itself. A rise in pressure stretches afferent smooth muscle cells and opens stretch-sensitive nonselective cation channels. The cells depolarize, voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ enters, and the arteriole constricts within seconds. A fall in pressure relaxes it. Besides stabilizing flow, this response keeps surges in systemic pressure from reaching the glomerular capillaries.

Tubuloglomerular feedback works more slowly and senses the result of filtration rather than pressure. The macula densa is a plaque of cells in the wall of the thick ascending limb where it passes between the afferent and efferent arterioles of its own glomerulus. Its cells take up NaCl through the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2), so their signal tracks the NaCl concentration of the fluid reaching them, which rises when GFR rises.

blocks.title: Tubuloglomerular feedback
steps: GFR rises in one nephron
More NaCl reaches the macula densa
NaCl enters macula densa cells through NKCC2
ATP is released and converted to adenosine
Adenosine on A1 receptors constricts the afferent arteriole
Glomerular pressure and GFR fall back toward normal
blocks.caption: A negative feedback loop: the response opposes the original change in GFR.

blocks.text: When NaCl delivery falls, the loop runs in reverse. Less adenosine is made, and the macula densa produces nitric oxide and prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole and stimulate renin release from the granular cells. The resulting angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, which also helps restore glomerular pressure. Blocking NKCC2 with a loop diuretic shows the sensing step: the macula densa then behaves as if NaCl delivery were low, and renin secretion rises.

blocks.caption: Both act mainly on the afferent arteriole, so both protect glomerular pressure as well as flow.

blocks.text: Below the lower limit, the arterioles are already maximally dilated, so flow and GFR fall passively with pressure. This is why GFR drops in shock, and why strong sympathetic activity during hemorrhage can override autoregulation and divert blood away from the kidneys.

blocks.predict: Mean arterial pressure falls from 100 to 85 mm Hg, then to 55 mm Hg. Predict GFR at each step.
blocks.explain: At 85 mm Hg GFR stays near normal because the afferent arteriole dilates through the myogenic response and reduced tubuloglomerular feedback. At 55 mm Hg pressure is below the autoregulatory range, the arterioles cannot dilate further, and GFR falls with pressure.
blocks.check: The autoregulatory range and the reverse operation of tubuloglomerular feedback.

sections.title: Vasa recta, medullary hypertonicity, and medullary hypoxia

blocks.text: The loops of Henle and collecting ducts build an interstitial osmolality that rises from about 300 mOsm/kg at the corticomedullary junction to about 1,200 mOsm/kg at the papillary tip in humans. Blood must supply the medulla without carrying this solute away. The vasa recta do this by two features: their flow is slow, and they are arranged as hairpins. Flow through the vasa recta of the inner medulla is only about 1 to 2% of total renal blood flow.

The vasa recta are countercurrent exchangers. As descending vessels enter the increasingly hypertonic medulla, their blood loses water and gains NaCl and urea, so its osmolality approaches that of the interstitium near the tip. As the ascending vessels climb back toward the cortex, the blood gives the solute back and regains water. The exchange is passive, so blood leaving the medulla is only slightly hyperosmotic, and little solute is removed. The ascending vessels also carry away more fluid than the descending ones bring in, removing the water reabsorbed from the descending limbs and collecting ducts. The vasa recta do not create the gradient; they preserve it. Because the exchange is passive, it works only when flow is slow, and an increase in medullary blood flow washes solute out and lowers the maximum urine concentration.

The same arrangement handles oxygen. Oxygen diffuses from descending to ascending vessels and returns toward the cortex without reaching the deep medulla. In the outer medulla, active NaCl transport by the thick ascending limb consumes much of the oxygen that does arrive. As a result the medulla is hypoxic, and the papillary tip, at the far end of the supply line, has the lowest oxygen tension in the kidney. This makes the papilla vulnerable to anything that further reduces its flow, which is why papillary necrosis occurs in sickle cell disease, diabetes, analgesic nephropathy from long-term use of analgesic mixtures and NSAIDs (partly through loss of prostaglandin-mediated medullary vasodilation), and severe pyelonephritis with obstruction.

blocks.text: In sickle cell disease and sickle cell trait, repeated sickling destroys the vasa recta and the deep parts of the long loops. Countercurrent exchange and multiplication then fail, so urine cannot be concentrated much above plasma osmolality (hyposthenuria). This begins in childhood and can cause nocturia and enuresis. Painless gross hematuria from papillary infarction is a recognized complication of sickle cell trait.

blocks.predict: Why is the renal medulla one of the few sites where sickle cell trait causes disease?
blocks.explain: Trait cells contain about 40% HbS, which normally does not polymerize enough to sickle. The medulla combines low oxygen, high osmolality that concentrates hemoglobin, low pH, and slow flow, which together push even this amount of HbS past the threshold for polymerization.

sections.title: The left renal vein, its gonadal tributary, and left varicocele

blocks.text: The inferior vena cava (IVC) lies to the right of the aorta, so the two renal veins differ. The right renal vein is short and enters the IVC directly. The left renal vein is longer: it runs from the left hilum across the midline, anterior to the aorta and just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), passing through the angle between these two arteries to enter the left side of the IVC. Along the way it receives the left gonadal vein from below and the left suprarenal vein from above, often with a lumbar tributary.

blocks.title: Left versus right venous drainage
rows: Long; crosses anterior to the aorta below the SMA
Left renal vein, at about a right angle
Uncommon; raises concern for IVC obstruction
blocks.caption: The left gonadal vein shares the pressure of the left renal vein; the right gonadal vein does not.

blocks.text: The testis drains through the pampiniform plexus, which forms the testicular vein near the deep inguinal ring. A varicocele is dilation of this plexus, felt as a soft mass above the testis that enlarges on standing or straining. Most varicoceles are left sided, explained by the longer course of the left testicular vein, its right-angle entry into a higher-pressure renal vein, incompetent or absent valves, and compression of the left renal vein. An ordinary varicocele drains and collapses when the patient lies down, because gravity no longer opposes outflow.

Renal cell carcinoma, which arises from tubular epithelium, has a strong tendency to grow into the renal vein as a tumor thrombus and can extend into the IVC and even the right atrium. When a left-sided tumor fills the left renal vein beyond the entry of the gonadal vein, testicular drainage is blocked mechanically. The result is a new left varicocele that does not collapse when the patient is supine, because the obstruction persists in any position. In women the same mechanism dilates the left ovarian vein. A right-sided tumor causes a varicocele only if tumor thrombus obstructs the IVC where the right testicular vein drains, so a new right or nondecompressing varicocele also calls for imaging of the kidney and IVC.

The left renal vein can also be compressed between the aorta and the SMA (nutcracker phenomenon). Raised pressure in the vein causes hematuria from rupture of thin-walled veins into the collecting system, left flank pain, and a left varicocele or pelvic varices.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a varicocele
blocks.text: A 58-year-old man has a new left scrotal swelling, hematuria, and weight loss. The swelling feels like a bag of veins and stays full when he lies flat. First, ask what drains the left pampiniform plexus: the left testicular vein, into the left renal vein. Second, a varicocele that persists supine points to a fixed obstruction rather than valve failure. Third, hematuria and weight loss point to a renal mass. The most likely explanation is a left renal cell carcinoma with tumor thrombus in the left renal vein. If the same varicocele were on the right, the lesion would have to involve the IVC, because the right testicular vein drains there.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain the kidney's vascular behavior together. The series arrangement of afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, and second capillary bed lets the kidney adjust filtration from either end and links filtration fraction to reabsorption downstream. The juxtaglomerular apparatus ties single nephron GFR to the renin-angiotensin system, so the same cells that autoregulate flow also help set systemic blood pressure. Biochemistry enters through hemoglobin S: polymerization depends on oxygen tension, hemoglobin concentration, and pH, and the renal medulla pushes all three in the wrong direction.

Pathology follows from the anatomy. End arteries explain pale wedge-shaped infarcts, the medulla's position at the end of a slow, oxygen-poor supply explains papillary necrosis from several different causes, and the course of the left renal vein explains why a renal tumor appears as a scrotal sign. The arteriolar rules hold for moderate changes rather than extreme constriction, and the quoted numbers vary between textbooks.

summary: The kidneys receive about 20 to 25% of cardiac output, mostly to the cortex, so that plasma can be filtered, not to meet metabolic need.
Blood passes renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate, and cortical radiate arteries, then afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, and peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
Two capillary beds in series give a high-pressure filtering bed and a low-pressure, high-oncotic reabsorbing bed.
Segmental and interlobar arteries are end arteries, so emboli cause pale, wedge-shaped infarcts with the base at the capsule.
Afferent changes move RPF and GFR together; moderate efferent constriction raises GFR and filtration fraction while RPF falls.
Prostaglandin afferent dilation and angiotensin II efferent constriction defend GFR when perfusion is low.
Autoregulation holds flow and GFR between about 75 and 160 mm Hg through the myogenic response and macula densa tubuloglomerular feedback using adenosine.
Slow countercurrent flow in the vasa recta preserves medullary hypertonicity but leaves the papilla hypoxic.
Hypoxia, hypertonicity, acidosis, and slow flow cause sickling in the vasa recta, papillary necrosis, hematuria, and hyposthenuria, even in sickle cell trait.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, so renal cell carcinoma in that vein causes a left varicocele that does not collapse when supine.

verify: The autoregulatory range is quoted as about 75 to 160 mm Hg in Guyton and Hall (used here) and up to about 80 to 180 or 200 mm Hg in other sources; confirm the range NABNE expects.
Medullary flow figures differ by region: about 1 to 2% of renal blood flow for the inner medullary vasa recta (Guyton and Hall) versus about 10% for the whole medulla; confirm which figure is tested.
Approximate pressures (glomerular capillary about 60 mm Hg, peritubular capillary about 13 mm Hg) follow Guyton and Hall; other texts give lower glomerular values (about 45 to 50 mm Hg).
The number of segmental arteries is usually given as five but varies; the frequency of accessory renal arteries (about 25% in Moore) varies among anatomical series.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects eponyms such as Brodel's line for the avascular plane, or only descriptive terms.
The relative contributions of ATP and adenosine to tubuloglomerular feedback are still debated; adenosine on A1 receptors is the consensus board answer.
The proportion of varicoceles that are left sided is commonly quoted as about 80 to 90%; confirm if a figure is tested.
HbS content in sickle cell trait is quoted as about 35 to 45%; this chapter uses about 40%.
A schematic of the renal vascular tree and a vasa recta countercurrent diagram would help; requested diagram names for a future revision: renal-vascular-tree, vasa-recta-exchange.
